solution: The answer is some pairwise distance d, and a balanced split has bichromatic closest pair at least d exactly when every pair closer than d is monochromatic, i.e. when every connected component of the threshold graph on edges shorter than d lies wholly inside one team; so d is feasible iff the multiset of those component sizes has a sub-multiset summing to exactly n. Merging components can only shrink the set of reachable subset sums, so feasibility is monotone in d and no binary search is needed: sweep the edges in increasing length with a DSU (Kruskal), and just before absorbing each distinct length w test subset sum n over the current component sizes with a bitset DP, keeping the last w that passes. Those threshold components are identical to the components of any MST of the complete graph restricted to edges below the threshold (cut property), so only the 2n-1 MST edges matter and Prim in O((2n)^2) supplies them; the winning check's DP reconstruction names the blue team. Squared distances stay exact 64-bit integers (max 8e18) and sqrt is applied only when printing. Overall O(n^2 log n) time: Prim is O(n^2), sorting 2n-1 edges is O(n log n), and the at most 2n subset-sum checks cost O(n * n/64) each.
statement_summary: Given 2n distinct points in the plane with integer coordinates, the task is to split them into two teams of exactly n points each so that the smallest Euclidean distance between any two points on opposite teams is as large as possible. One must report that optimal distance together with the membership of one team, for n up to 500.
notes: Verified: all three samples reproduce exactly, and the MST-based solver, an all-pairs Kruskal variant and an exhaustive brute force over balanced partitions agree on 550 random small cases (n=1..5, including tiny integer grids, clustered points, collinear points and heavy-tie lattices); the emitted team's true minimum cross distance always equals the reported value. CPython solves a worst case n=500 in 0.39s. Deliberately NOT labelled binary-search-answer: feasibility is monotone so one COULD binary search the sorted distances, but the ascending Kruskal sweep answers it in one pass, and the corpus trap note on that label applies. Deliberately NOT labelled closest-pair: the quantity optimised is a bichromatic closest pair, but no closest-pair algorithm (divide and conquer or sweep) is used - distances are only edge weights. minimum-spanning-tree is kept at lower confidence because it is an optimisation, not a requirement: sorting all ~500k pairs and running the same DSU sweep also fits the limits; it is included because the intended framing is the minimum bottleneck spanning tree and the answer is always an MST edge. geometry is weak - the plane only supplies the metric. 'bitset-dp' appears in the corpus but is not a canonical key, so the bitset subset-sum check is covered by subset-sum + dynamic-programming (note that subset-sum does not imply the dynamic-programming family via the taxonomy's regex, hence listing it explicitly).
